Interest rates and bond yields are rising, making dividend stocks less enticing, since investors can earn high returns without having to buy income-producing stocks. But the good news is that this has led to many dividend stocks trading lower lately, pushing their yields higher in the process and potentially setting them up for big gains later on.

Three excellent dividend stocks that are absurdly cheap right now and that are trading below $100 include AT&T (NYSE:T), Pfizer (NYSE:PFE), and Zoetis (NYSE:ZTS). Here's why they can be excellent options for income investors to consider for their portfolios right now.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

AT&T

AT&T's business has been doing well this year, but there simply hasn't been a huge catalyst to make the telecom stock a hot buy. Investors are going elsewhere for high returns, and there are also concerns that Space Exploration Technologies Corp plans to turn Starlink into a major U.S. carrier, potentially disrupting the entire telecom industry.

Those worries have been weighing on AT&T's stock, which is down about 16% this year. Even the company's recent earnings report, as strong as it was, wasn't enough to turn its fortunes around. AT&T posted more than 5% revenue growth in the September quarter, a far higher rate than usual, which should have given investors renewed confidence in the business. But that hasn't been the case, at least for now.

The stock is trading around $21 right now, and its price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple of 11 is incredibly low. The S&P 500 average is much higher at 23. AT&T's stock also yields 5.3%, providing investors with an extra incentive to buy it today, as it's not only cheap with significant upside potential but also offers high recurring income.

Pfizer

Pfizer's stock has actually been doing well this year, a nice change from previous years when investors remained cautious despite its posting steady, strong results. But even at around $30, this is an undervalued stock.

The healthcare company has been investing in its growth over the years, and while it may take some time for those efforts to translate into stronger top-line growth, the market has been overly punitive, with Pfizer shares down more than 30% over five years.

Its P/E multiple of 39 looks high, but Pfizer has also been incurring nonrecurring expenses as it restructures its operations and aims to get leaner and more efficient. Based on analyst expectations of future earnings, its forward P/E multiple is incredibly low, at just 10. And at 5.8%, it offers an even higher yield than AT&T.

AT&T (T) Stock Looks Cheap Relative To Its Earnings Outlook

AT&T shares have pulled back sharply in recent weeks after a strong multi-year run, which puts fresh focus on whether the current US$20.85 price is fully supported by the earnings power of the business. With new customer additions, portfolio reshaping and big network investments all in motion, the key issue is how those moves translate into sustainable profits per share.

Over the past 3 years the stock has returned 58.8% which now puts real weight on the question of how closely the share price tracks the underlying earnings profile.

Management is sharpening the footprint around fiber and U.S. wireless and plans a new headquarters campus in Plano, moves that can influence long term margins, capital intensity and the timing of cash generation.

Your read on AT&T is one view; the desks covering it have another. See what analysts think AT&T's shares could be worth.

The issue now is whether AT&T's current valuation is justified by the earnings the company is producing today and is expected to produce in the years ahead.

If you want to test the same earnings question you are asking of AT&T across a broader set of ideas, scan through the 29 high quality undervalued stocks.

Is AT&T a Bargain on Earnings?

The P/E ratio is a useful lens for AT&T because earnings remain a key anchor for how investors look at large, cash generative telecom groups. On this measure, AT&T trades on a P/E of 10.7x, which is slightly below the 11.6x peer average and sits more clearly below the broader Telecom sector on 14.8x. Against a tailored fair P/E that reflects AT&T's specific mix of growth prospects, profitability, scale and risk, the current multiple appears on the low side rather than the high side.

Because management has raised its 2026 earnings outlook and is talking about adjusted earnings growth targets through 2028, the market multiple suggests investors are still applying a discount even with that backdrop in view. For anyone assessing AT&T today, the gap between the current P/E and the level implied by the fair value framework highlights a stock that the market prices more cautiously than that earnings profile alone might indicate. AT&T (T) is one of the stocks most watched by Zacks.com visitors lately. So, it might be a good idea to review some of the factors that might affect the near-term performance of the stock.

Shares of this telecommunications company have returned -16.3% over the past month versus the Zacks S&P 500 composite's -0.8% change. The Zacks Wireless National industry, to which AT&T belongs, has lost 3% over this period. Now the key question is: Where could the stock be headed in the near term?

Although media reports or rumors about a significant change in a company's business prospects usually cause its stock to trend and lead to an immediate price change, there are always certain fundamental factors that ultimately drive the buy-and-hold decision.

Earnings Estimate Revisions

Rather than focusing on anything else, we at Zacks prioritize evaluating the change in a company's earnings projection. This is because we believe the fair value for its stock is determined by the present value of its future stream of earnings.

Our analysis is essentially based on how sell-side analysts covering the stock are revising their earnings estimates to take the latest business trends into account. When earnings estimates for a company go up, the fair value for its stock goes up as well. And when a stock's fair value is higher than its current market price, investors tend to buy the stock, resulting in its price moving upward. Because of this, empirical studies indicate a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and short-term stock price movements.

For the current quarter, AT&T is expected to post earnings of $0.53 per share, indicating a change of +1.9% from the year-ago quarter. The Zacks Consensus Estimate has changed +4.8% over the last 30 days.

For the current fiscal year, the consensus earnings estimate of $2.38 points to a change of +12.3% from the prior year. Over the last 30 days, this estimate has changed +2.5%.

For the next fiscal year, the consensus earnings estimate of $2.56 indicates a change of +7.4% from what AT&T is expected to report a year ago. Over the past month, the estimate has changed +0.5%.

Having a strong externally audited track record, our proprietary stock rating tool, the Zacks Rank, offers a more conclusive picture of a stock's price direction in the near term, since it effectively harnesses the power of earnings estimate revisions. Due to the size of the recent change in the consensus estimate, along with three other factors related to earnings estimates, AT&T is rated Zacks Rank #3 (Hold).

title: Should You Buy AT&T Stock For Its Cash?

Should You Buy AT&T Stock For Its Cash?

AT&T (T) produced free cash flow over the last twelve months equal to 12.5% of its market value, compared with 4.3% for the median S&P 500 company. A cash yield that high usually means the shares trade below the value of the business, investors expect the company to get smaller, or heavy debt makes the shares small next to the cash. So which one is AT&T?

AT&T's Sales And Operating Profit Are Still Growing

AT&T looks less like a shrinking business than its yield suggests, though much of that yield reflects its heavy debt, a distinction that matters for anyone drawn to its cash. Shareholders own a portion of the free cash a company produces, whether the money is paid out or retained, just as they own a portion of its profit. Retained cash still belongs to the owners of AT&T. When investors give it credit, the share price typically follows, particularly when the cash is growing.

The company sells wireless phone service and home internet. Over the last twelve months, AT&T grew revenue 3.5%, following 2.0% growth in the prior twelve-month period. Its operating margin widened to 21.4% from 19.5% a year earlier.

The cash presents a different picture. Capital spending consumed 55.7% of the cash AT&T generated from operations over the last twelve months. Free cash flow, the money left after that spending, totaled $17.8 billion, down from $20.0 billion a year earlier.

AT&T also carries more debt than its shares are worth. The company held $167 billion in net debt at the end of September, compared with a market value of $143 billion. Measured against market value plus net debt, about $310 billion, the cash yield is about 5.7%.

Why AT&T's Debt Rose In The Third Quarter

Management said AT&T's debt rose against its earnings because the company bought spectrum licenses from EchoStar for $23 billion at the end of July. Based on the company's own measures, net debt reached 3.13 times adjusted EBITDA, an operating earnings metric, up from 2.68 times at the end of the second quarter. Over the last twelve months, interest expense totaled $7.47 billion, and operating income covered it 3.7 times.

One part of the business is shrinking by design. Management said service revenue from older copper-based services fell about 25% in the third quarter from a year earlier, as AT&T powers down copper and transitions customers to newer technology. Wireless service revenue grew 5% over the same period. The company also recorded a $2.6 billion non-cash charge in the third quarter tied to its agreement to sell AT&T Mexico.
